To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the double inoculation of seeds of grey velvet bean with rhizobia and AMF did not affect the productivity of the grey velvet bean or the productivity of the sweet potato.

The double inoculation of seeds of grey mucuna with rhizobia and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) can increase the ability to produce biomass of these legumes and multiply the population of AMF in the soil.

the double inoculation of seeds of Mucuna prurien with strains of rhizobia and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) did not increase the capacity of production of dry matter of Mucuna and did not multiply the population of AMF in the soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of the double inoculation with rhizobium and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) in the productivity of the sweet potato ( Ipomoea battatas ) in the succession with the mucuna ( Mucuna pruiriens ).
the effects of the dual inoculation of seeds of gray mucuna Mucuna prurien s with rhizobia and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) on the productivity of the crop.

the effects of inoculating seeds of M. pruriens with different doses of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and rhizobia on the biomass production of M. prurines and on the yield of I. batatas cv. Rosinha.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the double inoculation of Mucuna prurien with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and rhizobium, in the first stage of the experiment, did not influence the production of dry matter in the second stage, where sweet potato was cultivated in succession.
the double inoculation of mucuna with rhizobia and AMFs, at any dose, does not provide any advantage in the production of dry matter and tuber yield of potatoes.
the inoculation of Mucuna prurita s L. with AMF did not increase the biomass production and yield of the following crop, sweet potato.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of leguminous cover crops in association with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) and rhizobia is not a good option for the establishment of potato crops.

we are able to produce a large quantity of biomass from a leguminous cover crop (M. pruriens) in a short period of time (3 months), and that this biomass can be used as a substrate to inoculate the soil with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and/or rhizobia.

the use of legumes in crop-living system can be a strategy to reduce the use of chemical fertilizers, but it is necessary to evaluate the effect of these plants in the soil, as well as the effect of the inoculation with microorganisms, which can improve the performance of legumes and the soil quality.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of FMAs and rizobio as inoculants for mucuna is not economically viable for the farmer.
the use of a double inoculation of legume seeds with strains of rhizobia and arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) may increase biomass production and multiplication of AMF populations in soils.
we have shown that the combination of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi and Rhizobium can be used in a sustainable agriculture system, which can help to improve soil fertility and crop yield.
